A glossy red spiral staircase can be spotted through windows that face the buzzy part of DeKalb Street in Fort Greene, Brooklyn. The space became the Million Goods ‘s second shop after co-founder Matt Reyer, who lives nearby, spotting it when it was inhabited by a design studio. Gjergji Shkurti designed the Fort Greene outpost for Million Goods Reyer and fellow co-founder Drew Kaufmann brought on local architect Gjergji Shkurti, founder of Figure Ground , to convert the space. Whereas the original Million Goods in Greenpoint is condensed into a single level, the Fort Greene location gave the team more room to work with, with two levels and an expansive courtyard. The studio revamped a two-level space “I think this was more regal, whereas Greenpoint was a little bit more fun,” Shkurti told Dezeen, referring to the expansive Breccia Pernice stone countertop that forms the wine bar portion on the first level. Stripping the interiors back to their essentials, Shkurti organised the space to provide social areas and retail, integrating them stylistically but separating them physically, with the social spaces on the bottom floor and the retail above. Shkurti designed the space and fabricated the millwork The first-level bar and social space combines multiple different design languages into a contemporary New York style. Behind the bar, metallic speaker boxes were integrated into the custom casework, which was rendered in sapele wood finished in a peca tone. Bridge Street Sound did the sound system, integrating a large speaker directly into the face of the marble bar. Emeco bar stools by Philippe Starck line the bar, and these chairs were used with the wooden banquet seating that hems the space. A backyard takes cues from Brazilian brutalism The ceiling has a distinctly Japanese appearance, with fabric draped between wooden slats. This fabric and an additional layer of insulation were included for sound, but also, with an interesting effect, dampen the lighting from the fixtures above the fabric. A relatively large backyard space was given a central planter for a mature tree. The circular planter doubles as a bench and seating was integrated into the washed concrete walls around the space. Upstairs, a space was included for retail Shkurti said the backyard was designed to evoke Brazilian brutalism. A Louis Poulsen Flindt Plaza post is the centrepiece of the backyard space, rising from the custom pavers. The lighting company sponsored the store and its lamps and fixtures can be found throughout. The refinished facade of the historic low-rise building was refinished with the blessing of the local preservation boards, and the backyard-facing trim was given a red that aligns with the staircase in the front. In the front, the facade was kept black. Read: Safwat by Safwat balances “humor, clarity, and restraint” at Funny Bar in New York The spiral staircase at the front of the shop was original, but given siding and painted a bright red by local fabricator Wood Steel Stone . Wood Steel Stone also completed an impressive central display table on the upper floor that folds aluminium and wood into ply layers with aluminium on top. Upstairs, the original wood from the floors was refinished and used. The team knocked voids in a partition wall to place speakers Shkurti’s custom millwork appears again as casing for the clothing and goods on display, which Reyer described as contemporary and accessible. Through a portal door, a metal stand, also created by Wood Steel Stone was designed to function as both a point-of-sale location and a DJ booth for events. To the sides of the portal door, voids were cleared out to put additional speakers that face into the primary retail space. Above the custom display table is a Louis Poulsen pendant lamp designed to have a vintage look. An upstairs changing area doubles as a point-of-sale station and DJ booth From the upstairs, shoppers can see kids playing basketball on courts across the street, anchoring the location in the neighbourhood. Other recent stand-out interiors include Federico Stevanovich’s studio designed with Nama Studio in Mexico City . Litening bars are increasingly a site of interesting design. Prefer Hypebeast on Google Fashion Oct 7, 2026 2.3K Hypes 0 Comments Comments Save Text By Paul Heavener Share this article Fashion Oct 7, 2026 2.3K Hypes 0 Comments Comments Prefer Hypebeast on Google Save 1 of 9 Million Goods 2 of 9 Million Goods 3 of 9 Million Goods 4 of 9 Million Goods 5 of 9 Million Goods 6 of 9 Million Goods 7 of 9 Million Goods 8 of 9 Million Goods 9 of 9 Million Goods Summary Million Goods has opened its second location, in Fort Greene, Brooklyn The space includes two custom sound systems split across a ground floor bar and listening room, and an upstairs retail floor The store stocks brands like Nicholas Daley, OAMC Peacemaker, Soulland, Rold Skov, LC23, Berner Kühl, Ranra and ssstein Million Goods , a Brooklyn-based retail concept combining independent menswear, hi-fi, natural wine and cultural programming, has opened its second location in Fort Greene, Brooklyn. A roughly 2,100-square-foot space set inside a landmarked building, the new location ports the brand’s DNA from its original Greenpoint location further south in the borough. Founders Drew Kaufmann and Matt Reyer treated the project as an adaptive reuse, keeping the building’s tin ceilings, fireplaces, wood floors and spiral staircase rather than gutting the interior. The store is split into three areas of about 700 square feet each: a bar and listening room on the lower level, a retail floor upstairs and a garden at the rear, visible from the entrance through large windows at the back of the listening floor. The original spiral staircase connecting the two floors is now wrapped in red metalwork, while other details like pecan finished woodwork, honed stone surfaces and limewash paint compliment custom aluminum retail fixtures. Louis Poulsen PH 5 pendants and AJ Eklipta wall lamps illuminate the space while the sound comes Bridge Street Sound designed slim-profile speakers and Million Goods-developed dual-sided speakers, both tuned by Ojas collaborator and sound designer Mo Yasin. The upstairs retail floor carries labels including Nicholas Daley , OAMC Peacemaker , Soulland, Rold Skov, LC23, Berner Kühl, Ranra and ssstein , with Kaufmann and Reyer selecting pieces directly with each brand. Downstairs, the natural wine list centers on France, the Fort Greene location serving a broader by-the-glass selection than Greenpoint. Out back, the garden incorporates the existing trees into the built-in seating with a layout that references Brazilian Brutalism and Japanese garden design. Million Goods Fort Greene is now open Tuesday through Sunday from noon until 10 p.m. on Tuesdays and Sundays, 11 p.m. on Wednesdays, and 12 a.m. on Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays. The original Greenpoint store continues to operate at 88 Franklin Street. Opened ahead of this weekend’s Pride celebrations in New York, Love Thy Neighbor sits next to the landmark where a series of protests in 1969 became a pivotal moment in mobilising the Gay Rights Movement. The bar features free-form shapes that nod to queerness and individuality Founders Shigefumi Kabashima and Elias Popa, along with Wild Form Design Studio , wanted the bar and dining concept to pay homage to the history of this location, both through design and their approach to hospitality. “Guided by the ethos of no straight lines, Love Thy Neighbor celebrates the queer community, chosen family, and the joys of gathering and belonging,” said the team. Shelves behind the bar follow the “no straight lines” rule set out by the owners Just over the below-grade threshold, a concrete floor panel is gilded with a quote from Marsha P Johnson – a transgender woman who was a key figure in the Stonewall Uprising protests for LGBTQ+ rights, and who continued to fight for queer rights and representation throughout her life. It reads “No pride for some of us without liberation for all of us” in gold letters and includes her signature below. A series of banquettes is divided by sculptural partitions A single brick from the original Stonewall Inn is displayed in a niche at the end of the bar, representing those thrown at the police who raided the bar on 28 June 1969 during the uprisings. “These elements serve as understated reminders of the past, while reinforcing a bright future ahead,” said the team. A single brick from the original Stonewall Inn is displayed in a niche Elsewhere, the curvaceous walls and partitions form an intimate, cavern-like space for 40 guests, and nod to queerness and individuality. “The idea of ‘no straight lines’ became a guiding principle for us,” said Kabashima. “It reflects not only the design of the space, but also how we think about hospitality: fluid, open, and without boundaries.” Spotlights illuminate the bar counter and tables The sculpted surfaces carry warm beige tones across banquettes on the left-hand side, and the bar along the right. A curated selection of liquor bottles and glassware is displayed behind the bar on back-lit shelves, which slant and dip to continue the free-form visual language. The cocktail menu draws on Japanese bartending precision Spotlights illuminate the rounded bar counter and dining tables, directing focus to the food and drinks, while cove lighting traces the fluid edges around the space. In the rear bathroom, a recessed mirror appears to be carved from the thick plaster walls, the vanity has an equally textured edge and features a long, contoured basin, and bronze-hued faucets are suspended from the ceiling. Read: Architecture profession “must engage” in ensuring safety for trans people says Queerscapes founder Love Thy Neighbor’s highly inventive cocktail menu draws on Japanese bartending precision, and uses techniques like clarification, infusion and carbonation to create innovative ingredients like wasabi gin and homemade cola. Drinks are presented in delicate glassware, while Asian-influenced bar snacks and shareable plates are served on hand-crafted ceramics. The rear bathroom features a recessed mirror and a rough-edged vanity “We wanted Love Thy Neighbor to be a space where people from different walks of life can share a delicious meal, connect, and feel like they belong under one roof, at any time of day,” said Papa. “We want guests to feel a sense of freedom here, both in how they experience the space and how they connect with others,” added Kabashima. The basin is contoured and faucets hang from the ceiling Many queer spaces are under threat from a variety of social, urban and economic issues, and continued support is needed to protect venues used by the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer (LGBTQ+) community. The transgender community is particularly being targeted in the US and UK. The architecture profession “must engage” in ensuring safety for trans people, the founder of Queerscapes told Dezeen in an interview last year. The photography is by Aichan Mama. Brought to life by bartender and restaurateur Shigefumi Kabashima and chef Elias Popa, the intimate venue takes shape as an atmospheric evening cocktail destination, with daytime service forthcoming. At its core, the space is a celebration of the queer community and the joys of chosen family, anchored by a design ethos that embraces fluidity and rejects rigid boundaries. “The idea of ‘no straight lines’ became a guiding principle for us,” says Kabashima. “It reflects not only the design of the space, but also how we think about hospitality: fluid, open, and without boundaries. We want guests to feel a sense of freedom here, both in how they experience the space and how they connect with others.” A hand-shaped environment Collaborating with Jun Qin of Wild Form Design Studio , the founders stripped down traditional church architecture to create a contemporary environment. Vaulted archways and curved, sculpted booths envelop guests in a comforting embrace, grounded by a warm, monochromatic beige palette inspired by sand and earth. “We wanted the entire space to feel as though it was sculpted rather than conventionally assembled, so many of the walls, seating areas, ceilings, and curved transitions were created through hand-shaped cement work,” explains Qin. “The microcement surface finish helps unify the entire environment visually, while also preserving a soft and natural texture throughout the space.” Rather than relying on one dramatic focal point, the architecture relies on cohesive, custom-designed elements. From the niches to the lighting details, the organic curves create a calming, emotional experience. Details to discover at Love Thy Neighbor Throughout the space are details that honor history and community. A single brick from the original Stonewall Inn is embedded within the bar, while a quote from late activist Marsha P. Johnson, which reads “No Pride For Some of Us Without Liberation For All of Us,” is set into the floor at the entrance. “My goal with the space was to embrace our history, paying respect to the literal bricks laid down by our neighbors like the Stonewall Inn, and to create a space that felt warm, embracing, and inclusive,” notes Popa. “Hence, the highlighted brick in the wall at the end of the bar, pulled from Stonewall. A cheeky homage to our shared history.” He continues: “In design, I love when things are clandestine, objects are hidden and only revealed to those who know where to look. This whole bar is an exercise in restraint and subtlety. At the end of the day, we really wanted to create a space that feels transportive, like as soon as you step into the restaurant you feel like you aren’t in New York anymore—even for just a moment.” Posted In: News ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Related Posts Five on Friday: October 30th, 2026 Chef Thomas Straker Brings His London Restaurant to New York La Fontaine Set To Debut in Century City Early 2027 Marcel Wanders Makes the Case for Taking Risks General News Projects Products Podcast People Resources Topics Hotels + Resorts Food + Beverage Development Interviews Event News Business + People Resources Webinars Downloads About Us About Us Advertise with Us Contact Us Contact Us Address: 100 Broadway 14th Floor, New York , NY 10005 Social: Follow Follow Follow Follow Follow © 2026 Emerald X, LLC. Rockwell Group ‘s Los Angeles office designed the Skywalker Grill without a single 90-degree angle, continuing the sweeping curves of the building by MAD Architects . The Skywalker Grill features no 90-degree angles to echo the Lucas Museum’s biomorphic architecture The eatery also references the warm cherry wood interiors of Skywalker Ranch, a 4,700-acre filmmaker’s retreat and workspace owned by Star Wars director George Lucas in Marin County, California. Overlooking the Los Angeles skyline, the fifth-floor restaurant and bar is named after the sci-fi media franchise’s principal character. It is open to both museum visitors and the general public for lunch and dinner. Entry to the fifth-floor space is via a corridor wrapped with cherry wood panels “Responding to the museum’s distinctive biomorphic architecture, the restaurant features no 90-degree angles,” said the Skywalker Grill team. “Curved walls are wrapped in individually crafted cherry wood panels, with no two panels alike, while finger-raked cherrywood columns echo the tambour banquettes lining the perimeter of the room.” Shimmering tiles cover the front of the snaking bar, while the back bar is clad in illuminated Corian Guests arrive via elevator to a corridor that leads to the host stand, lined on one side with cherry panelling that folds up and over the ceiling. Booths are formed with swooping partitions that organically rise and fall in height, and curve to create intimate pockets for conversation. The cherry used throughout the restaurant is a nod to the wood found at George Lucas’s Skywalker Ranch in Marin County A central island is ringed by a green crushed velvet banquette that matches the booth upholstery, and surrounded by circular tables and freestanding dining chairs in soft grey. Tamboured cherry-wrapped columns rise at slight angles and branch like tree trunks to meet the ceiling, which opens in the middle to reveal a beige plaster surface illuminated by cove lighting. A large ovoid window opens onto a terrace with panoramic views The snaking, glossy white bar counter is fronted by shimmering fluted tiles covered in crystal silver leaf, while illuminated Corian forms the back bar. A large ovoid window features operable glass panels that provide access to the outdoor terrace, where further seating enjoys views over the University of Southern California campus towards Downtown LA. Read: MAD’s spaceship-like Lucas Museum revealed ahead of opening “The design incorporates elements of cinematic storytelling, including framing, light, scale and atmosphere, while pairing high-tech materials with handcrafted details,” said the team. The restaurant’s American-style menu features California-grown ingredients, including Wagyu beef and honey ricotta sourced from Skywalker Ranch. Curved, undulating partitions form intimate dining booths Set in a 13-acre landscaped site near Los Angeles’ Exposition Park, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is dedicated to storytelling and features a variety of galleries, theatres and educational spaces. MAD and Stantec wrapped the building in over 1,200 curved panels, creating an extraterrestrial form that wouldn’t look out of place in one of Lucas’s beloved movies. The terrace enjoys panoramic views over Los Angeles Rockwell Group is known for its theatrical hospitality projects that immerse diners in atmospheric spaces. Other recent examples include an art deco-influenced Manhattan steakhouse , a revolving restaurant above Times Square and a “cathedral of fried chicken” . The photography is by Tom McGovern . Designed by Rockwell Group and operated by Rhubarb Events & Hospitality Collection , part of Oak View Group (OVG) , Skywalker Grill draws inspiration from the welcoming spirit of George Lucas' legendary Skywalker Ranch, pairing classic American cuisine with warm hospitality and sweeping views overlooking Los Angeles. Open to both museum visitors and the public, Skywalker Grill welcomes guests for lunch, dinner and weekend brunch, offering a natural extension of a museum visit as well as a place to gather for an evening meal. Remaining open beyond museum hours, the restaurant invites guests to enjoy panoramic views of Los Angeles long after the galleries have closed. “Skywalker Grill is a natural complement to the Lucas Museum experience, offering an inviting space for guests to connect over great food and conversation before or after visiting our galleries,” said Tracey Bates, CEO of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art. “We are equally excited for it to serve as a destination for Angelenos from across the city to enjoy exceptional hospitality and beautiful surroundings.” Skywalker Grill offers a menu that reflects California-grown ingredients and the enduring appeal of classic American cuisine. Guests can begin with shareable favorites such as Dungeness Crab Cakes and Lobster Corn Dogs, before enjoying signature entrées including Crispy Chicken Milanese, Honey Miso Glazed Salmon and the Skywalker Ranch Wagyu Burger. House-made pastas, fresh seasonal salads and shareable starters round out a menu that is both refined and approachable. "We are incredibly honored to have been part of this remarkable project, and we set out to create a dining experience worthy of it. The menu is inventive yet approachable, designed to welcome everyone. The restaurant's beautiful interiors and thoughtful service were conceived to make it a true Los Angeles destination: a warm, museum-minded hospitality experience that keeps Angelenos and visitors coming back again and again. It is both a tribute to the museum's creative energy and a wonderful reason to dine out," said Katie Harel, Managing Director, Rhubarb Hospitality Collection / Oak View Group Hospitality. Designed by Rockwell Group’s Los Angeles office, Skywalker Grill blends contemporary and Midcentury Modern influences with sculptural architectural forms to create a dining experience that feels both timeless and inviting. Cherry wood wraps the restaurant's walls and ceiling in individually crafted panels, creating warmth and texture throughout the dining room, while softly illuminated white onyx Corian surfaces introduce a subtle sense of light and movement. At the center of the space, a sculptural bar anchors the restaurant, surrounded by intimate seating areas designed to foster conversation and connection. The design extends beyond the main dining room to include an elegant private dining room with switch-glass walls that transition from clear to frosted for added privacy, as well as an outdoor terrace nestled among lush landscaping, offering guests panoramic views of Los Angeles in a relaxed, garden-like setting. "The Lucas Museum celebrates the power of storytelling, and we wanted Skywalker Grill to become part of that narrative," says David Rockwell, Founder and President, Rockwell Group. "Our design echoes the museum’s craftsmanship and innovation while introducing moments of intimacy, warmth, and surprise. From the glowing Corian surfaces to the handcrafted cherry wood detailing, every element was designed to create a sense of wonder that feels tactile and welcoming." Earlier this month, the filmmaker, along with his wife Mellody Hobson, gave America an otherwordly new cultural destination, The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art – and a restaurant, Skywalker Grill. The restaurant sits at the top of Ma Yansong's otherworldly new building. And like the museum's broader mission, Skywalker Grill is all about the power of visual storytelling, not to mention fresh takes on classic American fare. With views over downtown Los Angeles and references to Lucas' famed Northern California workplace Skywalker Ranch, the destination provides an out-of-this-world place to unwind after a day traipsing through galleries. Here's what to expect. (Image credit: Tom McGovern) Wallpaper* dines at Skywalker Grill The Mood: A galaxy far, far away Designed by Rockwell Group’s Los Angeles office, the restaurant features a generous open floor plan, defined by green-hued leather and velvet banquettes tucked into undulating timber room dividers. The sweeping dining room opens out onto a large dining patio with breathtaking city views. According to firm founder David Rockwell, the design language borrows from midcentury modernism and the idea that architecture can also tell stories. ‘We wanted the restaurant to feel connected to George Lucas’ world through materiality, craftsmanship, imagination and an optimism about the future of design,’ Rockwell says. (Image credit: Tom McGovern) While there are touches of luxe materials throughout (like a bar clad in silver gilt), cherry wood is the primary material, a stylish foil to the building's futuristic space-age envelope; no two panels are alike, thanks to the meticulous work of a local fabricator. ‘The continuous curves and sculpted transitions give the room a sense of movement,’ Rockwell adds. ‘George is naturally drawn to midcentury design and cherry wood is a featured material in his warm and inviting Skywalker Ranch. The 529-key Kimpton Era is housed within a purpose-built, 33-storey tower on West 48th Street, just south of the art deco Rockefeller Center complex. The Kimpton Era’s blackened-steel staircase spirals up through a three-storey fluted atrium For the interiors, INC pulled in references from New York City itself, blending Uptown elegance and Downtown grit, as well as the compact grandeur of the luxury liners that once docked along the Hudson. “Every detail of the Kimpton Era is engineered elegance with a room that feels more like a stateroom on an ocean liner – compact, crafted, and refined to the luxury of just enough,” said INC partner Adam Rolston. The reception area is anchored by a tiered black-stone counter Materials throughout were chosen to reflect the city’s dichotomy, pairing marbles, brass, leather and glazed ceramics with more industrial concrete and blackened steel. In a triple-height atrium wrapped in fluted concrete, a blackened steel-and-glass stair coils around a mobile of organic forms that descends from the ceiling. The second-floor brasserie featured panelled walls and mosaic flooring Cerused wood, terrazzo borders and diffused lighting define the elevator lobbies, while the tiered black-marble reception counter provides a weighted presence. “Inspired by the city itself, the Kimpton Era captures New York’s layered character — elegant yet gritty, refined yet raw – woven into a vertical voyage of venues and comfort in a purpose-built skyscraper at the heart of Rockefeller Center,” said INC’s Hillary Kroll. Terracotta-toned walls and ceramic pendants add texture in the restaurant spanning the ground and cellar levels The hotel’s five dining venues include a Latin American eatery with terracotta walls and ceramic pendants that spans from the ground floor to the cellar. A second-floor brasserie features banquette seating, panelled walls, a scarlet ceramic bar and mosaic floors, while the third-floor lobby cafe offers coffee in the mornings and cocktails at night. Read: INC creates “gritty yet inviting” interiors for restaurant in The Spiral skyscraper On the roof, a bar references the dining rooms of Chinatown via a tomato-red counter framed by tiled portals, temple-like joinery and hand-painted lotus motifs. The Kimpton Era’s guest rooms are designed like compact ship cabins, with each “berth” featuring full white-oak walls that integrate a bed, desk and storage into a single furniture element. White oak millwork integrates multiple furniture pieces in the guest rooms Neutral colour palettes are offset by jewel-toned fabrics and brass accents, while wet-room-style bathrooms are defined by frosted, blackened metal-framed sliding glass doors that conserve space. “[The Kimpton Era] is a self-contained voyage where guest rooms are like staterooms and lounges, and dining rooms unfold like the salons of a great ocean liner in a new expression of New York luxury,” said INC’s Louisa Revitte. Jewel-toned fabrics enliven the otherwise neutral rooms INC’s previous hotel projects have included the 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge with Marvel Architects, and the event spaces at the TWA Hotel inside Eero Saarinen’s JFK Airport terminal. The studio – which celebrates its 20th anniversary this year – has also completed “gritty yet inviting” interiors for a restaurant in BIG’s The Spiral skyscraper, and filled its own concrete-forward offices with eclectic furniture and plants. Located below an early 20th-century house in the Mexican capital’s historic colonia, Libreria Valladolid was designed to evoke the experience of exploring old bookshops. Photo by Rene Villaseñor Photography Previous Next Photography Close “It captures the thrill felt when entering these places, searching for a unique story that has patiently waited among thousands of books on all topics and from many eras,” said Em-Estudio . Accessed from the street through an unassuming door, the entry vestibule features shelves packed with old volumes and more stacks along a wooden staircase that descends to another threshold. Photo by Rene Villaseñor Small lamps are squeezed between the spines and placed on top of the stacks, creating a moody glow that sets the scene for the bar beyond. “The old bookstore is encountered upon entering, as you descend the stairs, and it remains behind as you cross the first threshold, where the books transform into the skin that embraces the rooms,” said the studio. Inside the basement, dark herringbone flooring and surfaces drenched in burgundy continue the bookshop atmosphere. The larger walls are lined entirely with shelves filled with books stacked spine inwards, so the warm beige of their pages faces the room. Cove lighting illuminates the books, creating a dramatic contrast with the otherwise shadowy bar, while banquettes below are accompanied by circular marble tables for placing drinks. “The pages of thousands of books resting on bookshelves that reach the ceiling shed their literal meaning, becoming a tapestry in shades of white that only time can give, bathed in a gradient of warm light,” Em-Estudio said. Other areas such as the DJ booth, the bar and the bathrooms are highlighted with gold leaf and brass to draw the eye. A further hidden lounge space is disguised by another bookshelf, decorated with cans and objects that “evoke a grocery-store bar”. This room swaps burgundy for green, applied in gloss across the ceiling and appearing in a long marble table that runs through the centre. Read: Mexico City restaurant by RA! arranged around upside-down pyramid bar Dark wood Van Beuren chairs with yellow upholstery are lined up along each side, parallel to more walls of books that are uplit along each shelf. A mirror that covers the back wall visually doubles the space, extending the table and the bookshelves in the reflection. Em-Estudio was co-founded by architect Ivan Esqueda and interior designer Gala Sánchez-Renero – a husband and wife who also operate individual practices. Their previous collaborations include a holiday home on a steep hillside in Oaxaca, Mexico, built from coloured concrete chosen to blend into the rocky mountainside. When designing the project, NM3 drew on the influential design of Loos’s famous bar , an early modernist landmark finished in 1908. Photography Previous Next Photography Close “The American Bar was more of an aspiration than a direct formal reference,” studio co-founder Francesco Zorzi told Dezeen. “The ambition was never to recreate Loos’s bar, nor Robert and Trix Haussmann’s Kronenhalle in Zurich, which was another important reference for the project,” he explained. “Rather, we wanted to create a truly classic bar for Milan, with a very specific spatial and architectural character.” Located just across the road from the city’s popular Bar Basso , Bar Bardo is housed within a 55-square-metre single room with an additional bathroom. Almost every element in the listening bar was custom-designed by NM3, known for its modernist-style stainless steel furniture that has already made the young studio a household name in Milan since its founding in 2020. The walls and ceiling were clad with polished rosewood panels, which add character to the small space while improving its acoustics. A quintessentially NM3 stainless steel bar was placed in the centre of the room, where its gleaming surfaces reflect globular 1950s pendant lights by Italian architect Luigi Caccia Dominioni. The lamps are the only vintage pieces in the bar. NM3 swapped their original chains for longer black ones. Photo by T-Space The perimeter of the space features built-in red velvet banquette seating, which matches crimson curtains and a series of bright red speakers fitted across the bar to accommodate a stainless steel DJ booth and metal shelving for vinyl records. Bar Bardo was purposefully designed to be a flexible space. Every interior element is movable, with the exception of the bar and the banquettes. Read: “Progressive spirit” of Space Age interiors informs Barcelona cocktail bar “By simply removing the furniture, the cocktail bar can easily be transformed into a club,” said Zorzi. “The flexibility of the space is therefore achieved through a simple architectural arrangement rather than complex spatial interventions.” At the back of the space, the striking bathroom was covered with bright red 10-centimetre-by-10-centimetre tiles, from floor to ceiling. Photo by T-Space Utilitarian stainless steel was once more selected for the toilets, sink and other fixtures, while pared-back sconce lights illuminate the cubicles. Bar Bardo marks a softer design direction for NM3. The studio previously conceived a “raw” interior for Milan’s Galleria Montegani , as well as a similarly metal-heavy store in the city for fashion brand Miss Sixty. Ahead of Milan design week in April, NM3 was among the studios that spoke to Dezeen about what it’s like to be a contemporary designer in Italy’s design capital. The team has completely redesigned Peak with Priceless , the restaurant located on the 101th floor of the KPF-designed 30 Hudson Yards skyscraper. The interiors of Peak by Priceless have been redesigned so every seat has an uninterrupted skyline view The overhaul also includes the addition of Avenue Sky Lounge – a revival of the popular Avenue nightclub in Chelsea, which shuttered in 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic and never reopened. Susan Nugraha, Tao Group Hospitality ‘s SVP of design and development, worked closely on the project with experiential design group Journey . Custom tiered lighting nods to art deco skyscrapers such as the Empire State Building Both hospitality concepts draw design influences from the Manhattan skyline visible through the wraparound, floor-to-ceiling windows. “The inspiration behind Peak and Avenue was always New York itself, its energy, glamour and unmistakable sense of occasion,” said Journey managing director David Taglione. “Suspended above the city with the skyline as its stage, we wanted to create a hospitality experience that feels both elevated and deeply connected to the rhythm of New York.” Soft blue and warm brown suede covers the booth seating References to art deco structures such as the Empire State Building and Rockefeller Center can be spied in tall, tiered lamps, customised to softly illuminate both Peak and Avenue spaces. “Every design decision, from the rich materiality to the layered seating and subtle Art Deco references, was shaped to frame the view while creating a space with its own distinct sense of presence,” said Taglione. Read: Edge sky deck protrudes from supertall Hudson Yards skyscraper At Peak, stepped booths are oriented towards the views, while smaller tables run along the windows – ensuring every seat has an unbroken sightline. Soft blue and warm brown suede upholster the curved seat backs, with wavy patterns echoed in partitions that run along the back of the dining space Avenue Sky Lounge (also main image) continues the same colour palette A similar colour palette appears across Avenue Sky Lounge , which can be divided into more intimate spaces by coffee-hued curtains that follow arched ceiling features. Lacquered wood panelling surrounds the bar, where more geometric shapes in the stone counters and liquor display cases again nod to art deco. “Our vision was a design that is both timeless and of the moment, seamlessly adapting to any time of day or occasion,” said Nugraha. Lacquered wood panelling and geometric details around the bar again nod to the city’s art deco icons The revamp at The Edge will also see the return of Marquee Skydeck , a series of events that include DJ sets and performances on the platform that at 1,100 feet (335 metres) above street level is currently the highest observation deck in the western hemisphere. Other sky-high hospitality venues in New York City include Manhatta , a Woods Bagot-designed restaurant atop 28 Liberty in the Financial District. The photography is courtesy of Tao Group Hospitality. items.text: How This New Orleans Hotel Went From Former Haunted House to Chic Destination | Architectural Digest Skip to main content AD PRO DIRECTORY APPLY NOW Architectural Digest Architectural Digest DIRECTORY ARCHITECTURE + DESIGN SHOPPING CELEBRITY AD IT YOURSELF AD PRO Menu Menu Search Menu Menu Directory Architecture + Design Shopping Chevron Celebrity AD It Yourself AD Pro Chevron Real Estate Lifestyle MORE VIDEO THE MAGAZINE NEWSLETTERS Search Search Architectural Digest Search Close Menu Menu Menu Ghost Host How a Coven of New Orleans Design Diehards Transformed This Haunted House Into a Hot Hotel An exclusive look at New Orleans’s most intriguing new design hotel, The Whit—and its scandalous, high-camp backstory By Lauren Mechling Photography by Frank Frances Styled by Sara Mathers October 30, 2026 The newest addition to the New Orleans design hotel scene, The Whit, has a history of local scandal, hauntings, and high-camp decor Frank Frances Studio Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story The Greek Revival mansion that sits at the corner of Prytania Street and Jackson Avenue in New Orleans’ Garden District wouldn’t know “dull” if it came up and rang the doorbell. The 1857 building’s first owner was a cotton merchant who died of yellow fever. Another owner was fatally struck by lightning. Fast-forward to the 21st century, when a Tina Turner impersonator bought the property and turned it into Magnolia Mansion, a B&B with suites with names like Vampire Lovers’ Lair and Moulin Rouge. A former professional boxer and local politics kingmaker took over, but things fell apart around the time of the FBI’s raid on the property. Oh, and the estate is said to be haunted . The Whit's moody mahogany-paneled library Frank Frances Studio The hotel's parlor Frank Frances Studio Named in its B&B era by USA Today as one of the top places in the nation “to sleep with a ghost” the magisterial Harris-Maginnis House earned a spot on the city’s ghost-tour circuit with an ever-mounting pile of lore. According to a spooky tour-operator website , guests at the B&B reported various eerie happenings over the years, such as the sensation of somebody tucking them in at night or a presence watching them while they slept. There were also rumblings of mysterious footsteps and slamming doors. Ghosts or no ghosts, the new team taking over the place found gothic-coded wall murals and dark purple velvet hanging at every turn. Who you gonna call to give an old haunt a new design vernacular? Gretchen Trauth, CEO of the New Orleans investment firm behind the New Orleans hotel, rang up Jensen Logan and Katie Leblanc Killen of Logan Killen, a local design firm known for infusing spaces with a beguiling mix of polish and patina. “The goal was a hotel where nobody can quite tell whether a designer has touched it,” says Logan. Breakfast room with Pierre Frey wallpaper Frank Frances Studio “We wanted it to feel very storied, like it’s been someone’s house for a long time,” adds Killen. “There are these layered histories imbued in the furnishings and the art and accessories.” Named for poet Walt Whitman, who spent three months in New Orleans around the time of the home’s construction, the designers have reimagined the property with a romantic, lived-in, and curio-studded aesthetic that tempts guests to sit down and stay awhile. Architect Seamus McGuire of New Orleans firm Cicada helped navigate historical codes and redraw the map to capture some of the glamour that had drained away in recent years. His blueprint called for converting a trio of bedrooms into lounges. A mahogany-paneled library is now a gallery of antique dog portraits and a repository of volumes from local independent Faulkner House Books. “It’s dark and moody, and where you might want to have a cocktail or a whiskey,” Logan says of the clubby room. Bookworms might also gravitate to the sunroom’s banquette seating, one of the wicker chairs on the wraparound porch , or the breakfast room , a delightfully matchy-matchy enclave covered in Pierre Frey Les Colonnes wallpaper and curtains. The Whit's porch Frank Frances Studio The hardest room to get right, say the designers, was the main lounge. “It’s a giant space that isn’t always in use, and can be tricky to give life to when it’s empty,” says Killen. Intended to serve as a great room by day and an atmospheric cocktail bar come evening, the team layered in elements such as blue paint that reads ethereal by day and warm by night, a custom grid carpet to add a sense of tailoring to the expansive area, and an intimate salon-style wall of works by Louisiana artists, including Robert Moreland and Mallory Page. Another tightrope walk was the second-floor bar. Landmark rules forbid faking history a space never had, so the team went openly Deco instead. “What we don’t want is to put a contemporary bar into a very historic property,” says McGuire. “You can’t give a false sense of history to a space.” One of the hotel's 15 guest rooms Frank Frances Studio It will probably come as little surprise that the bedrooms resist uniformity. In addition to the classically designed units, a quartet of cozy garden rooms has low ceilings and glossy oxblood walls; three cabana rooms feel airy, with bamboo beds and high ceilings. “It’s not meant to feel like everything was changed by the same person at the same time,” Killen says of the narrative that she and Logan have introduced to the New Orleans hotel. As for the supposed ghosts, nobody’s heard boo.
